analysis.one_liner: Requires utilities to reach 20% renewable electricity by 2024, extended clean energy tax credits, and raised taxes on major oil companies to help pay for it.
analysis.headline: Introduced with bipartisan sponsorship in February 2008, the bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, never received a vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required large electric utilities to steadily increase the share of power they get from wind, solar, geothermal, biomass, and other renewable sources, from 2% in 2010 up to 20% by 2024. It would have extended and expanded a wide set of tax credits for renewable electricity, home solar and small wind systems, energy-efficient homes and appliances, biodiesel, and electric vehicles. To offset the cost, it would have taken away a major tax deduction from the biggest integrated oil companies and imposed new taxes and fees on offshore Gulf oil and gas production.
analysis.who_benefits: Homeowners who install solar panels, small wind turbines, or energy-efficient equipment would get larger and longer-lasting tax credits. The wind, solar, geothermal, and biomass industries would gain a guaranteed, growing national market for their electricity, plus extended production and investment credits. Electric utilities would be guaranteed recovery of their compliance costs from customers.

how_it_helps.text: Requires electric utilities selling more than 4 million megawatt-hours a year to obtain a rising share of their electricity from renewable sources, starting at 2% in 2010 and reaching 20% by 2024, with small utilities and Hawaii exempted.

Extends and expands tax credits for renewable electricity production, clean renewable energy bonds, residential solar and small wind property, energy-efficient homes and appliances, biodiesel, cellulosic and small ethanol producers, and plug-in electric vehicles.

Offsets the cost of these incentives by denying major integrated oil companies the domestic production tax deduction, increasing and extending the Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund tax, and imposing new taxes on crude oil and natural gas from the Gulf of Mexico outer Continental Shelf.

Allows alternative compliance payments of 2 cents per kilowatt-hour and places the proceeds in a fund for state renewable energy and conservation grants, and includes provisions for homeowners, rural areas, and generation on Indian land.

Allows double credits for renewable generation on Indian land and triple credits for small distributed generators no larger than 1 megawatt, and allows utilities to recover prudently incurred compliance costs from customers.

analysis.who_pays: Major oil companies would pay through the loss of a large tax deduction and new taxes on offshore Gulf production, though part of this could be passed to consumers at the pump. Electric utilities and their customers would bear compliance costs, which the bill allows utilities to recover in rates. The extension of the ethanol tariff through 2011 would keep cheaper imported ethanol off the market, a cost borne by fuel buyers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Major oil companies, utilities, fuel buyers

drawbacks.text: The renewable electricity requirement and its 2-cents-per-kilowatt-hour alternative compliance payment would raise electricity costs, and the bill explicitly requires regulators to ensure utilities recover those compliance costs from customers.
Extending the tariff duty on ethanol until 2011 protects domestic ethanol producers from cheaper imported ethanol, which raises fuel costs for consumers.
New taxes and fees on oil companies and on Gulf of Mexico offshore production could be passed through to consumers in gasoline and heating prices.
The bill relies on an extensive set of extended and new tax credits whose cost is offset only by the oil-related tax provisions, leaving little room for error if those offsets were changed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered a concrete national path to cleaner electricity plus immediate tax help for homeowners investing in efficiency and renewables, paid for substantially by narrowing oil company tax breaks. Its real costs are modest but real: somewhat higher electric rates, higher fuel prices from the ethanol tariff, and possible pass-through of oil taxes. The design favors established incentive channels, and it extends protectionist support for corn ethanol alongside genuinely forward-looking provisions, so its value depends on weighing a broader clean-energy transition against those narrower protections.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee in February 2008 and sat there without a hearing, a markup, or a vote until the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Senator Amy Klobuchar introduced the bill on February 14, 2008, together with Senator Olympia Snowe and Senator Maria Cantwell.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the day it was introduced.
No further action was taken; the bill never left the Finance Committee and received no floor vote before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Major oil companies kept their domestic production tax deduction and avoided the new offshore taxes, and electric utilities faced no federal renewable electricity requirement. Renewable energy developers went without the extended federal tax credits this bill would have provided.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil companies and utilities; no federal mandate

industries.industry: Renewable electricity producers (wind, solar, geothermal, biomass)
industries.note: The bill creates a guaranteed national market for their electricity through the 20%-by-2024 standard and extends the production and investment tax credits they depend on. Their interest in the bill ran alongside the public interest in cleaner power, though consumers would pay part of the cost through rates.

The bill would have denied them the domestic production tax deduction and imposed new taxes on Gulf of Mexico offshore production to fund the renewable incentives. The oil industry's loss was the bill's funding mechanism, and its gain from the bill dying was the public's lost opportunity.

Utilities would face a federal renewable electricity mandate and civil penalties for noncompliance, but small utilities and Hawaii are exempt, and the bill guarantees recovery of prudently incurred compliance costs from customers. They could pass most of the cost to ratepayers.

The bill extends the tariff on imported ethanol through 2011, locks in the small ethanol producer credit, and extends biodiesel credits, keeping cheaper foreign ethanol off the market. Consumers paid the difference at the pump while the industry's protected position continued.

The bill extends and expands the expensing election for refineries, including those processing shale and tar sands, even as it raises taxes on integrated oil producers. Consumers would bear new taxes that could be passed through in fuel prices.

industries.industry: Home efficiency and clean-vehicle equipment makers
industries.note: Extended credits for residential solar and wind, energy-efficient homes and appliances, alternative-fuel refueling property, and plug-in electric vehicles would create customer demand for these products while lowering homeowners' energy bills.
